headline: Decode an OID from its bytes, find a certification path a rotated CA hides, and refuse the key-possession requests the linter let through.
summary: Correctness fixes across three areas. `pki.asn1.decodeOidContent` took its length from a property a caller can set independently of the bytes, so it could return an OID the buffer does not encode, and an OID selects an algorithm. `pki.sigstore.verifyBundle` assembled a certification path by taking the first intermediate matching an issuer name, so a bundle carrying two intermediates with one subject, which is what a rotated CA looks like, was refused for want of a chain it carried. And the RFC 9883 key-possession surface read one attribute of several and one field where the requirement turns on two, so `pki.possession.verifyRequest` accepted requests it should refuse, `pki.lint.csr` graded conforming what that verb rejects, and `pki.csr.sign` emitted them under a profile that advertises the requirement.

Fixed: `pki.altSig.verify` and the other `pki.altSig` verbs checked which format their input was without checking that it is a well-formed one of that format, then read extensions out of it directly. A certificate carrying the `altSignatureValue` extension twice was therefore verified successfully: the verb read the first of the two and the preimage it reconstructed removed both, while `pki.schema.x509.parse` refuses the same bytes with `x509/duplicate-extension`. The structure is parsed before any extension is read, so every rule the shared parser enforces holds here too.

`pki.possession.verifyRequest` and `pki.possession.statementOf` read only the first `statementOfPossession` attribute of a request that carries several, so every binding check on the rest was skipped. A request carrying a sound statement followed by one naming a different certificate was accepted on the strength of the first. A request carrying more than one is now refused with `possession/bad-request` at both doors, which is what `pki.schema.csr` and `pki.cms` already did for the attribute sets they read.

`pki.possession.verifyRequest` read only the first `extensionRequest` attribute of a request that carries several, and every check RFC 9883 asks for reads the extensions a request asks for. A request naming `keyAgreement` in its first attribute and `digitalSignature` in its second was therefore reported as not requesting a signature certificate, which is the section 6 prohibition, and a later subjectAltName request could escape the section 3 comparison the same way. Which attribute a CA should honor is stated nowhere, so a request carrying more than one is now refused with `possession/bad-request`, as `pki.schema.csr.decodeExtensions` already refused it.

`pki.possession.verifyRequest` did not treat a DSA subject key as signature-only, so a request to certify one, which can only ever sign, did not engage the RFC 9883 prohibition the way an EdDSA, RSASSA-PSS, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA key does. DSA is now in that set.

`pki.lint.csr` under the `rfc9883` profile graded conforming two requests that `pki.possession.verifyRequest` refuses, so `pki.csr.sign(..., { profile: "rfc9883" })` emitted both although the profile advertises the requirement. A request whose subject key can only ever sign, naming no keyUsage at all, met neither the sec. 4 requirement that "the subjectPKInfo MUST contain the public key for the key establishment algorithm" nor the sec. 6 prohibition on obtaining a signature certificate, and was reported as having no findings; the row read only the key usages a request asks for. A request carrying more than one `statementOfPossession` attribute was likewise unreported, and which of several a CA should honor is stated nowhere, so every check the section asks for would have been made against one statement while the CA certified a request carrying another. Both are now errors, `lint/rfc9883/signature-certificate-requested` and the new `lint/rfc9883/statement-attribute-repeated`, and the linter and the verifier read one table of the signature-only key algorithms.

`pki.possession.verifyRequest` compared the subject alternative names a request asks for against the signature certificate's by rendering each entry to a string, so one comparison rule stood in for every GeneralName form. A dNSName differing only in case reported `subjectAltNamesMatch: false`, and so `valid: false`, although RFC 4343 makes DNS comparison case-insensitive; an rfc822Name differing only in the case of its host and a URI differing only in the case of its scheme or host did the same; and a directoryName re-encoded to equivalent bytes read as a second name although RFC 5280 sec. 7.1 compares one attribute at a time. Each form is now compared under its own rule, so the pairs that differ only where their rule folds match, and the pairs that differ where their rule is exact, an rfc822Name local part and a URI path among them, still do not. A form with no comparison rule of its own is compared by its encoded bytes, and a value a rule cannot be applied to is reported as unmatched rather than resolved either way.

The RFC 9883 citations named the wrong sections. The prohibition "The privateKeyPossessionStatement attribute MUST NOT be used to obtain a signature certificate" is in section 6, not section 4, and the two name comparisons whose resolution the RFC leaves to the certificate policy are in section 3, not section 4. The refusal messages `pki.possession.verifyRequest` reports, the `citation` field of `lint/rfc9883/signature-certificate-requested`, and the CRMF proof-of-possession note, which belongs to section 5, now each name the clause they enforce.

`pki.jose.verify` read a supplied JWK's `crv` eight times and its `kty` nine times on one successful verification, and the first of those reads is what selects which curve the Edwards low-order point check validates the key against. A caller object answering that read differently from the later ones therefore had its key checked under one curve's parameters and imported under another: a JWK whose `crv` answered `Ed448` once and `Ed25519` afterwards verified, with the point check bypassed. That check is what stops a low-order key from verifying a forged signature. The key is now copied once, before any member of it is read, so the check, the import and the algorithm selection all read one key; a key whose members are accessors is refused as `jose/bad-key`.

`pki.jose.sign` read `opts.key` four times: once to test that it is a key, twice for the check that binds the key's hash to the header's `alg`, and once more to sign with. A caller object answering those reads differently had the binding checked against a key that did not sign, and the signed message then declared an algorithm its signature was not made under. The RSA algorithms were where it showed, since the registry's fixed signature widths catch the HMAC and elliptic-curve cases and two 2048-bit RSA keys produce the same signature length. A conforming verifier rejects such a message, including `pki.jose.verify`, so it is not a signature another party accepts; what was wrong is that the key the check approved was never the key that signed. The option is read once now, before anything inspects it, and the hash check, the signing and the width check all read that one key. A key whose `algorithm.hash` disappeared between two of those reads previously produced an untyped `TypeError` from a public verb rather than a `jose/*` fault.

`pki.jose.thumbprint` checked each JWK member and then read it again to build the hash, so the RFC 7638 identifier could be computed over values the checks never approved. The thumbprint is how `pki.jose.verify` decides that an embedded key and a supplied key are the same key, and how an ACME key authorization names an account, so an identifier over unchecked values names a key that was never validated. The key is copied once at the door. The published RFC 7638 and RFC 8037 known answers are unchanged.

`pki.tuf.checkExpiry` read `metadata.expires` three times: once to check it is a date string, once for the comparison, and once for the refusal message. A caller object could pass the type check with one date and hand the comparison a later one, and the verb then returned `true` for metadata that had expired. Expiry is the freeze-attack check, so a true verdict there answered about a date the document does not carry. The field is read once.

`pki.tuf.keyId` validated a key's `keytype`, `scheme` and `keyval` and then hashed the key, reading every field a second time. The identifier it returns is what a role's `keyids` list authorizes, so a key could validate as one shape and be hashed as another, naming a key that never passed validation. The key is copied before it is validated, and a key whose members are accessors is refused as `tuf/bad-key`.

`pki.acme.validate` read each field three times, for the closed status enum, the refusal message and the type check, while a conditionally-required field's predicate read the object again. A caller object could therefore pass the status enum as `valid`, answer the predicate so that a required field became optional, and present a third value to the type check, and the object was reported as conforming. Every field is now read once, before any check runs, and all of the checks decide from that reading. `pki.acme.validateProblem`, `pki.acme.identify` and `pki.acme.validateRenewalInfo` each read a member twice and now read it once; a non-string reaching the second read previously produced an untyped `TypeError` rather than an `acme/*` fault. The object is still returned as supplied.

The `pki.acme` request builders validated an option and then serialized it into the payload they sign, reading it twice, so a caller object could satisfy the validator with one value and have the signed request carry another. `revokeCert` is the sharpest case: the RFC 5280 CRLReason check exists to exclude the single unassigned value 7, and that is the value which could reach the certification authority. The same gap put unvalidated contacts, identifiers and dates into signed `newAccount`, `newOrder`, `newAuthz`, `updateAccount`, `challengeResponse`, `deactivate` and `postAsGet` payloads, so the mailto hygiene, the RFC 3339 checks and the boolean gates these verbs document were each enforced against a value that was never sent. Every one of them now passes its options through the gate the client methods already used, which refuses an options object whose fields are accessors rather than reading them once. The client methods were never affected.

`pki.acme` client `renewalWindow` validated `opts.previous` before fetching renewal information and read it three more times afterwards, so the prior window its stickiness decision compares against need not have been the one validated, and a value that stopped being an object across the fetch produced an untyped `TypeError`. The option is read once, before the fetch.

`pki.tlog.inclusionProof` read its `read` callback twice, once to check that it is a function and once to fetch tiles with, so the function checked need not have been the function called. The callback is read once.

The numbers `pki.ct`, `pki.sigstore` and `pki.webauthn` read as integers are now held to denoting exactly the integer they are read as. A token written `1.0000000000000001` becomes the number 1, so an integer check made after parsing sees a conforming document, and for a signed tree head that value is folded back into the bytes the signature covers: the rounded spelling verified while the value reported was not the one the log sent. The same applies to a Sigstore log index and integrated time, which enter the canonical form a signed entry timestamp covers, and to a FIDO metadata `no`, which is the rollback counter a relying party compares against the catalogue it already holds. An integer too large to represent exactly is refused for the same reason, since `9007199254740993` reads back as `9007199254740992`.

These are ordinary JSON formats where exponent form is legal, and nothing a conforming producer may emit is refused: `1e3`, `1.0` and `1500e-2` are read as their integers, and fields that are genuinely fractional are untouched. The rule names the members it applies to rather than the document, because these formats carry fractional values elsewhere by design: a FIDO metadata statement states biometric false-reject and false-accept rates as fractions, and an in-toto predicate inside a Sigstore bundle is arbitrary JSON.

A `tree_size` of `1.5` is now `ct/bad-json` rather than `ct/bad-sth`: a token that does not denote an integer is a malformed document, while one that denotes an integer the field cannot take, such as `-1`, is still a bad tree head.

`pki.tlog.verifyCheckpoint` read `opts.origin` four times, to see whether it was supplied, for its type, for its length, and for the comparison against the checkpoint. An accessor answers each read separately, so a caller object could present one origin to all three checks and the checkpoint's own origin to the comparison: the pinned origin was never the origin enforced, and the verdict reported a checkpoint as matching a log it does not name. The option is read once and the checks and the comparison both read that.

`pki.tuf.verifySignatures` read `opts.role` four times, for the presence check, the type check, and then each of `keyids` and `threshold`. `role` carries the authorization, so an accessor could present a strict role to the checks and a lax one to the field reads, combining one role's authorized keys with another's threshold: a document carrying one signature was reported `verified` against a role that required two. The role is captured once and every field is read off that capture.

`pki.tuf.canonicalJson` encoded any object by its own enumerable keys, so a `Date`, a `Map` and a `Set` each became `{}` and a Buffer became a map of its byte indices. Canonical JSON is the preimage a TUF signature covers, so a field encoding to `{}` is a field the signature does not cover while it remains in the caller's document: the signed form and the document the caller believes they signed differed, with nothing reporting it. The encoder already refused a float, a function, `undefined`, a BigInt, `NaN` and `Infinity`; a built-in object is now refused the same way. Plain objects, including null-prototype records, and arrays are unaffected.

An HPKE context dropped its additional authenticated data instead of binding it, when that data was held in a `DataView` or an `ArrayBuffer`. `context.seal` and `context.open` decided whether to bind the AAD by testing `aad.length`, which is `undefined` for both containers, so the AEAD was set up with no additional data and the tag authenticated none. Both sides dropped it alike, so the message still opened and a caller exercising their own code saw the round trip succeed while the binding they relied on was absent: a ciphertext could then be opened under any other AAD. The AAD is now normalized before its width decides anything, so it binds whichever container holds it, and a message sealed under one AAD no longer opens under another. An absent or empty AAD still means no additional data, as RFC 9180 sec. 5.2 specifies. `pki.cms` and `pki.webcrypto` were unaffected: the CMS additional data is the DER this toolkit builds, and the WebCrypto surface already normalized it.

`pki.crmf.verifyPop` read the first `statementOfPossession` control of a request that carries several and returned, so every later statement went unchecked: a request whose first statement is sound and whose second names a different certificate reported `verified: true` on the strength of the first. Which control a certification authority should honor is stated nowhere, so a request carrying more than one is now refused with `crmf/bad-controls`, as `pki.possession.verifyRequest` already refused the equivalent PKCS#10 attribute. A repeated CMS signed attribute was already refused by the shared parser; a CRMF control is a different structure and was not.

`pki.crmf.build` did not recognize a `statementOfPossession` supplied through the pre-encoded `controls` array, only through the object form, so it resolved the proof-of-possession algorithm from the key being certified rather than from the signature certificate the statement names. Building an X25519 request with a pre-encoded statement therefore failed with `crmf/unsupported-algorithm` while the identical request in object form succeeded. Both forms now resolve the signing certificate the same way, and a pre-encoded statement that does not decode, or that omits its certificate, is refused with `crmf/bad-controls` rather than passed over.

Byte-taking verbs across the toolkit accepted a Buffer and a `Uint8Array` but refused a `DataView` or an `ArrayBuffer` carrying the same bytes, although each advertises the whole set and one names it outright: "ikm must be a byte source (Buffer / TypedArray / DataView / ArrayBuffer)". An `ArrayBuffer` is what `Response.arrayBuffer()` and `crypto.subtle.exportKey("raw", ...)` return, so the refused half is the half a caller is most often holding, and the refusal blamed the content for the container. In `pki.tlog` it was worse than a refusal: `parseTile`, `parseNote`, `parseEntryBundle`, `parseCheckpoint` and `keyId` threw a bare `TypeError` with no code for an `ArrayBuffer`, so a caller could not branch on it and a fuzz harness could not tell it from a crash. Fixed at `pki.tlog` (all five verbs), `pki.hpke` (`info`, `aad`, plaintext, `ikm` and the exporter context), `pki.sigstore.verifyBundle` (the pinned `rekorKeys` and `ctLogs` material), `pki.tuf.verifySignatures` (`metadata.signedBytes`), `pki.ct` (the pinned log key on `getSth`, `getProofByHash` and `fetchLogList`, the SCT fields, and an issuer named by its SubjectPublicKeyInfo) and every format's `decodeExtension`. The size cap still runs before any copy, because normalizing shares the caller's buffer rather than duplicating it. Shared memory stays refused, and a key is still a `KeyObject`, a Buffer or the `{ pkm }` wrapper, which the refusal now names exactly instead of saying "a raw buffer".

`pki.path.crlChecker` and `pki.path.ocspChecker` take a list. Handed a single CRL or response, which is the natural slip, they mapped over whatever arrived: a `DataView`, an `ArrayBuffer` or a plain object produced a bare `TypeError` naming an internal expression, and a single CRL Buffer was mapped over its bytes and reported the first byte as a malformed CRL. Both now refuse a non-list with `path/bad-input` naming the argument. An omitted or empty list still means there is nothing to check.

`pki.tlog.verifyNote` and `pki.tlog.verifyCheckpoint` chose the digest for an ECDSA signature from the key's curve, so a conforming note signed by a P-384 or P-521 log key was refused with `tlog/bad-signature` and only P-256 logs interoperated. Signature type `0x02` is defined by c2sp.org/signed-note as "ECDSA signatures as implemented by github.com/transparency-dev/witness", whose verifier computes a SHA-256 digest for every key it accepts; the digest belongs to the signature type, not to the key. All three curves the specification admits are now verified under SHA-256, and a signature made with the digest the curve would suggest is refused. The curve allowlist is unchanged: a key on any other curve is still `tlog/bad-input`.

`pki.asn1.decodeOidContent` read its byte count from the input's `length` property. A Buffer accepts an own `length` that differs from its real size, and every other read of a buffer's bytes, indexing, `subarray`, `concat` and `toString`, uses the real count; only `length` can disagree. So a buffer whose bytes encode `1.2.840.3` and whose `length` reported 3 decoded as `1.2.840`, handing back an OID the bytes do not encode while an OID selects a signature algorithm and an extension decoder. The count is now taken once from the authoritative source, so the bytes decide.

The check that every internal fail-closed guard declares how its shape is kept from being re-inlined read a module's exported names with a pattern that recognized `module.exports = {` and `module.exports = Object.freeze({`. The guard modules export through a freeze reached by another name, so the check read 18 of the 19 as exporting nothing and passed over every function in them: 13 guards had no declaration and nothing said so. The pattern now matches the wrapper as any callee, and the 13 declarations are in place. No shipped behavior changes; the gate that was meant to prevent a guard shipping without enforcement now does.

`pki.sigstore.verifyBundle` refused a bundle whose certificate chain carries more than one intermediate with the same subject where only one of them is the real issuer, which is the shape a CA key rotation produces. Three things had to change, and together they make the verdict independent of the order the bundle lists its certificates in. The search now backtracks instead of taking the first intermediate matching an issuer name, as `pki.path.build` already did. It offers every path it finds rather than one, so an intermediate that matches by name and then fails validation no longer hides the sibling that would have validated. And it tries a candidate that completes the path before one that does not, so a chain padded with same-subject intermediates cannot consume the search. The work is bounded: at most 8 paths, 256 search steps and a depth of 16, so a chain carrying many same-subject intermediates is abandoned rather than explored.
